Lauren, Zoe, Carson, Sofia
Kenzo (luxury) is owned by LVMH and was acquired in 1993. Founder Kenzo Takada sold his eponymous fashion house for 
approximately $80 million.
●
Statements / values: The LVMH Supplier Code of Conduct addresses key areas including respect for human rights, business 
ethics, environmental responsibility, data protection, and diversity and inclusion.
●
Re-KENZO: “Re” refers to concepts of rebirth, renewal, and respect. The Re-KENZO project is a limited initiative consisting 
of casual, intentionally gender-fluid T-shirts made from existing stock materials.
●
Kenzo is not rated highly by Good On You.
●
The brand received a score of 21–30% in the 2021 Fashion Transparency Index.
●
Kenzo partnered with WWF to create a capsule collection aimed at supporting efforts to double the global wild tiger 
population by 2022, following a decline of over 95%.
○
This capsule collection, developed in collaboration with WWF, was designed to raise awareness and funds to support 
tiger conservation. All garments were produced using certified organic cotton.
●
Realities not aligned: Levi’s vs. Kenzo trademark lawsuit.
●
Sourcing: Bags are produced in Italy; footwear is manufactured in Spain and Portugal.
○
The company sources 48% of its leather from Leather Working Group–certified suppliers, meaning that approximately 
half of its leather sourcing is not certified.
○
Kenzo used 27% renewable energy across its own facilities in 2018 and set a target of reaching 30% by 2020.

Nigo
Nigo’s appointment in 2021 was a strategic move by LVMH. As a Japanese 
creative rooted in streetwear and pop culture, Nigo reconnects Kenzo with the 
brand’s original DNA established by Kenzo Takada, while modernizing it for a 
younger generation.
This decision reflects the evolution of Parisian luxury, where streetwear is now 
recognized as a legitimate creative force. Nigo’s background with BAPE 
positions Kenzo as a bridge between luxury heritage and global youth culture, 
highlighting how fashion history is increasingly shaped by cultural crossovers.
●
Appointed Artistic Director in 2021 by LVMH
●
Founder of A Bathing Ape (BAPE)
●
Strong connection to global streetwear & youth culture
●

●

Kenzo Takada

Rebranding
●
Shift from aggressive tiger logo
●
Introduction of the KENZO “Boke Flower”
●
Inspired by a Japanese flower that blooms in winter
●
Used as print, embroidery, patch, and logo
●
Softer, playful, optimistic identity
●
Connects Japanese culture + Parisian fashion
●
Strong visual consistency across collections
 In his first collection, SS22, Nigo introduced the Boke Flower to 
redefine Kenzo’s visual identity. Moving away from the aggressive tiger 
motif, the flower represents softness, joy, and resilience, while 
referencing Japanese culture and Nigo’s heritage. Its playful and graphic 
style still fits within a Parisian luxury context.
This rebranding is effective because the Boke Flower acts as a 
recognizable signature across clothing, accessories, and digital 
platforms. Similar to Chanel’s camellia, it creates strong visual 
consistency, appeals to Gen Z and millennials, and supports 
Kenzo’s shift toward a more approachable and culturally driven 
luxury identity.

Recent Collections- A homecoming or homage 
 “We are going back home, back to the beginning,” — 
Nigo
•The FW26 show took place at Kenzo Takada’s former 
home in Paris, reinforcing a return to the brand’s 
origins and sense of heritage
•The collection felt folkloric but classic and luxe, with 
Japanese tailoring meeting Western modern style and 
cultural influences blending naturally
• Key references such as the Kite bag, bicoloured suits, 
and Yankee-style elements nodded to classic Kenzo 
while reworking them in a contemporary way
• Kenzo feels increasingly commercial, but Nigo’s 
intent to realign the brand’s legacy is clear through 
forward-thinking, wearable designs that resonate with 
younger generations, raising the question of whether 
the brand might sit more naturally on the womenswear 
schedule

E-Commerce
Kenzo’s website is curated to be very simplistic to show off their creative pieces. Their website 
follows the design of other fashion sites, like Farfetch and Jacquemus. All of these e-shops are 
very fast and responsive, and excel on these three aspects:
Usability
●
These website is simplistic, easy to navigate, and layout neatly that customers know 
where to find what they are looking for. 
Design
●
Offering a sleek and minimalist design adds to each brand's image of luxury, causing 
minimal confusion while navigating shopping. 
Conversion Funnel
●
The process of selecting products, adding them to the cart, and checking out is seamless 
and easy for any age category of consumers, ensuring a smooth shopping experience
One point of Kenzo’s e-shop that they could work on is when someone adds an item to their cart, 
to advise shoppers to add some of their goodies to their bag as well to boost their sales. This 
could be from a piece of jewelry or a keychain, which overtime could garner them a lot more 
sales.

Digitization
Since its inception, Kenzo has had their finger on the pulse when it 
comes to adaptability. As a brand that came into Parisian fashion 
with their unique colors and patterns, they have paved a way for 
themselves by meeting their consumers needs. Kenzo has turned 
from offering their products in store to offering a hybrid shopping 
experience, giving their consumers the option for both the in store 
and online experiences. 
In the same manner, their use of social media and over digital 
avenues has allowed them to access new markets that might have 
been unattainable before. Their dedication to brand storytelling 
combined with their drive for innovating themselves to meet 
consumer demands has led them to this point of offering a 
well-balanced hybrid experience.
